# 0. The task and the Lab 4 pipeline

**Prediction task (as in Lab 4):** will this TNBC patient die of disease? The
prediction is made at the tumour board after surgery and tumour profiling,
before adjuvant therapy is decided. The positive class is **Died**.

This section rebuilds the Lab 4 pipeline with the same seeds: split first,
`mice` fitted on the training rows only (a random forest for tumour stage, which
won the masking experiment in Lab 4), then encoding, near-zero-variance filter,
training-only scaling, correlation filter, information gain and RFE.

```{r pipeline-data}
cl <- read.csv("tnbc_clinical.csv", na.strings = c("NA", ""), check.names = FALSE,
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mu <- read.csv("tnbc_mutation.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(cl)[1] <- "PATIENT_ID"; names(mu)[1] <- "PATIENT_ID"
genes <- setdiff(names(mu), "PATIENT_ID")
dat <- merge(cl, mu, by = "PATIENT_ID", sort = FALSE)
dat$y <- factor(ifelse(dat$VITAL_STATUS == "Died of Disease", "Died", "Living"),
                levels = c("Living", "Died"))

clean_lv <- function(f, signs = FALSE) {
  lv <- levels(f)
  if (signs) lv <- gsub("-", "neg", gsub("\\+", "pos", lv))
  levels(f) <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", lv); f
}
typed <- function(d) {
  out <- data.frame(
    AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS = as.numeric(d$AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS), NPI = as.numeric(d$NPI),
    TUMOR_SIZE = as.numeric(d$TUMOR_SIZE), MUTATION_COUNT = as.numeric(d$MUTATION_COUNT),
    GRADE = factor(ifelse(is.na(d$GRADE), NA, ifelse(d$GRADE == 3, "3", "1-2")),
                   levels = c("1-2", "3"), ordered = TRUE),
    TUMOR_STAGE = factor(ifelse(is.na(d$TUMOR_STAGE), NA,
                                ifelse(d$TUMOR_STAGE <= 1, "0-1", as.character(d$TUMOR_STAGE))),
                         levels = c("0-1", "2", "3"), ordered = TRUE),
    CELLULARITY = factor(d$CELLULARITY, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high"), ordered = TRUE),
    ER_IHC = factor(d$ER_IHC), LATERALITY = factor(d$LATERALITY),
    BREAST_SURGERY = factor(d$BREAST_SURGERY),
    INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE = factor(d$INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE),
    CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE = factor(d$CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE), HER2_SNP6 = factor(d$HER2_SNP6),
    INTCLUST = factor(d$INTCLUST), THREEGENE = factor(d$THREEGENE),
    COHORT = factor(d$COHORT))
  out$INTCLUST  <- clean_lv(out$INTCLUST, signs = TRUE)
  out$THREEGENE <- clean_lv(out$THREEGENE, signs = TRUE)
  out$CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE <- clean_lv(out$CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE)
  out$BREAST_SURGERY  <- clean_lv(out$BREAST_SURGERY)
  out
}
numeric_v <- c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "MUTATION_COUNT")
ordinal_v <- c("GRADE", "TUMOR_STAGE", "CELLULARITY")
nominal_v <- c("BREAST_SURGERY", "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE", "LATERALITY", "ER_IHC",
               "CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE", "HER2_SNP6", "INTCLUST", "THREEGENE")
X <- typed(dat)

set.seed(2026)
s  <- sample.split(dat$y, SplitRatio = 0.7)
tr <- which(s); te <- which(!s)
ytr <- dat$y[tr]; yte <- dat$y[te]
rbind(train = table(ytr), test = table(yte))
```

```{r pipeline-impute, cache=TRUE}
st   <- rbind(X[tr, ], X[te, ])
ign  <- c(rep(FALSE, length(tr)), rep(TRUE, length(te)))
meth <- make.method(st); meth[] <- ""
meth[numeric_v] <- "pmm"
meth[c("GRADE", "CELLULARITY")] <- "polr"
meth["TUMOR_STAGE"] <- "rf"
meth[c("ER_IHC", "LATERALITY")] <- "logreg"
meth["THREEGENE"] <- "cart"
meth[colSums(is.na(st)) == 0] <- ""
imp <- suppressWarnings(mice(st, m = 5, maxit = 10, method = meth, ntrees = 100,
                             predictorMatrix = make.predictorMatrix(st),
                             ignore = ign, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE))
Xc <- mice::complete(imp, 1)
```

```{r pipeline-features, cache=TRUE, dependson="pipeline-impute"}
make_feat <- function(Xcomp, rows) {
  f <- Xcomp[, c(numeric_v, ordinal_v, nominal_v)]
  for (o in ordinal_v) f[[o]] <- as.integer(f[[o]])
  cbind(f, dat[rows, genes])
}
feat_tr <- make_feat(Xc[seq_along(tr), ], tr)
feat_te <- make_feat(Xc[-seq_along(tr), ], te)
dv  <- dummyVars(~ ., data = feat_tr, fullRank = TRUE)
Etr <- predict(dv, feat_tr); Ete <- predict(dv, feat_te)
colnames(Etr) <- colnames(Ete) <- make.names(colnames(Etr), unique = TRUE)
nz <- nearZeroVar(Etr, saveMetrics = TRUE)
keep_nzv <- rownames(nz)[!nz$nzv]
pp  <- preProcess(Etr[, keep_nzv], method = c("center", "scale"))
Str <- predict(pp, Etr[, keep_nzv]); Ste <- predict(pp, Ete[, keep_nzv])
cm <- cor(Str)
drop_derived <- if (abs(cm["AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE.pre"]) > 0.8)
  "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE.pre" else character(0)
rest <- setdiff(colnames(cm), drop_derived)
corr_drop <- c(drop_derived, findCorrelation(cm[rest, rest], cutoff = 0.8, names = TRUE))
keep_corr <- setdiff(colnames(Str), corr_drop)

H <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log2(p)) }
ig1 <- function(x, y) {
  if (is.numeric(x) && length(unique(x)) > 2) {
    br <- unique(quantile(x, 0:4 / 4, na.rm = TRUE)); x <- cut(x, br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  }
  tab <- table(x, y); px <- rowSums(tab) / sum(tab)
  H(prop.table(table(y))) - sum(px * apply(tab, 1, function(r) H(r / sum(r))))
}
ig_vec <- function(M, y) sapply(seq_len(ncol(M)), function(j) ig1(M[, j], y))
set.seed(11)
M <- Etr[, keep_corr, drop = FALSE]
ig_real <- ig_vec(M, ytr)
null <- replicate(300, ig_vec(M, sample(ytr)))
ig_pass <- ig_real > apply(null, 1, quantile, probs = 0.95)
ig_keep <- colnames(M)[ig_pass][order(-ig_real[ig_pass])]   # same column order as Lab 4

set.seed(13)
xr <- as.data.frame(Str[, ig_keep, drop = FALSE])
sizes <- sort(unique(pmin(c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20), ncol(xr))))
rfe_fit <- rfe(x = xr, y = ytr, sizes = sizes, ntree = 300,
               rfeControl = rfeControl(functions = rfFuncs, method = "repeatedcv",
                                       number = 5, repeats = 3))
feats <- predictors(rfe_fit)
Atr <- as.data.frame(Str[, feats, drop = FALSE]); Ate <- as.data.frame(Ste[, feats, drop = FALSE])
```

```{r pipeline-check}
feats
```

Features were chosen on the training rows only. RFE ranks them with random
forests, which could give the forest a small advantage in this comparison, and I
keep that in mind below.

# 1. Four models on the same training data

All four see the same five features, the same rows and the **same 5-fold, 5-repeat
cross-validation folds**. Each is tuned by cross-validated ROC-AUC on the training
rows. The test rows are used once, at the end.

```{r fit, cache=TRUE, dependson="pipeline-features"}
set.seed(100)
folds <- createMultiFolds(ytr, k = 5, times = 5)
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", index = folds, classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary, savePredictions = "final")
set.seed(101)
m_glm <- train(x = Atr, y = ytr, method = "glm", family = binomial(), metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl)
set.seed(101)
m_tree <- train(x = Atr, y = ytr, method = "rpart", metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
                tuneGrid = data.frame(cp = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1)))
set.seed(101)
m_rf <- train(x = Atr, y = ytr, method = "rf", metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
              tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = 1:4), ntree = 500)
set.seed(101)
sig <- as.numeric(sigest(as.matrix(Atr), scaled = FALSE)[2])
m_svm <- train(x = Atr, y = ytr, method = "svmRadial", metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
               tuneGrid = expand.grid(sigma = sig, C = 2^(-2:4)))
models <- list("Logistic regression" = m_glm, "Decision tree" = m_tree,
               "Random forest" = m_rf, "SVM (radial)" = m_svm)
```

```{r tuning}
lapply(models[-1], function(m) m$bestTune)
```

## Cross-validated performance on the training rows

This is what I use to **choose** a model. The test table below is for
**reporting**; choosing the winner from test scores would make its test score
optimistic.

```{r cv-table}
cv_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(n) {
  r <- models[[n]]$resample
  data.frame(model = n, cv_ROC_AUC = mean(r$ROC), cv_ROC_sd = sd(r$ROC))
}))
cv_tab[, -1] <- round(cv_tab[, -1], 3)
cv_tab[order(-cv_tab$cv_ROC_AUC), ]
```

# 2. Metrics table on the same test data

Every metric is written from the predicted probabilities in base R.

```{r metrics-fns}
confusion <- function(p, y, thr = 0.5) {
  pred <- p >= thr; pos <- y == "Died"
  c(TP = sum(pred & pos), FP = sum(pred & !pos), TN = sum(!pred & !pos), FN = sum(!pred & pos))
}
safe <- function(a, b) if (b == 0) 0 else a / b
roc_auc <- function(p, y) {                      # P(random positive ranks above random negative)
  r <- rank(p); n1 <- sum(y == "Died"); n0 <- sum(y == "Living")
  (sum(r[y == "Died"]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
pr_curve <- function(p, y, w_neg = 1) {          # one point per distinct score, ties handled together
  th <- sort(unique(p), decreasing = TRUE)
  pos <- y == "Died"
  do.call(rbind, lapply(th, function(t) {
    tp <- sum(p >= t & pos); fp <- w_neg * sum(p >= t & !pos)
    data.frame(thr = t, recall = tp / sum(pos), precision = tp / (tp + fp),
               fpr = sum(p >= t & !pos) / sum(!pos))
  }))
}
pr_auc <- function(p, y, w_neg = 1) {            # average precision: sum of precision x recall step
  k <- pr_curve(p, y, w_neg)
  sum(diff(c(0, k$recall)) * k$precision)
}
all_metrics <- function(p, y, thr = 0.5) {
  m <- confusion(p, y, thr); TP <- m[["TP"]]; FP <- m[["FP"]]; TN <- m[["TN"]]; FN <- m[["FN"]]
  sens <- safe(TP, TP + FN); spec <- safe(TN, TN + FP)
  c(accuracy = (TP + TN) / sum(m), balanced_accuracy = (sens + spec) / 2,
    sensitivity = sens, specificity = spec, F1 = safe(2 * TP, 2 * TP + FP + FN),
    ROC_AUC = roc_auc(p, y), PR_AUC = pr_auc(p, y))
}
```

```{r test-table}
probs <- lapply(models, function(m) predict(m, Ate, type = "prob")[, "Died"])
base_p <- rep(mean(ytr == "Died"), length(yte))   # majority-class baseline: always "Living"
probs_all <- c(list("Majority-class baseline" = base_p), probs)
metric_mat <- t(sapply(probs_all, all_metrics, y = yte))
knitr::kable(round(metric_mat, 3), caption = "Test set, threshold 0.5. Positive class = Died.")
conf_mat <- t(sapply(probs_all, confusion, y = yte))
knitr::kable(conf_mat, caption = "Confusion counts on the test set")
prev <- mean(yte == "Died"); n_test <- length(yte)
c(test_patients = n_test, died = sum(yte == "Died"), prevalence = round(prev, 3))
```

## How uncertain are these numbers?

The test set is small, so I bootstrap the test patients 2,000 times.

```{r boot, cache=TRUE, dependson="fit"}
set.seed(200)
idx <- replicate(2000, sample(seq_along(yte), replace = TRUE))
idx <- idx[, apply(idx, 2, function(i) length(unique(yte[i])) == 2)]
bs <- lapply(probs, function(p) apply(idx, 2, function(i)
  c(ROC = roc_auc(p[i], yte[i]), PR = pr_auc(p[i], yte[i]))))
ci <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(bs), function(n) {
  q <- apply(bs[[n]], 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
  data.frame(model = n, ROC_low = q[1, "ROC"], ROC_high = q[2, "ROC"],
             PR_low = q[1, "PR"], PR_high = q[2, "PR"])
}))
rownames(ci) <- NULL
```

```{r boot-show}
best_cv <- cv_tab$model[which.max(cv_tab$cv_ROC_AUC)]
ci[, -1] <- round(ci[, -1], 3)
knitr::kable(ci, caption = "95% bootstrap intervals on the test set")
diffs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(setdiff(names(probs), best_cv), function(n) {
  d <- bs[[best_cv]]["ROC", ] - bs[[n]]["ROC", ]
  data.frame(comparison = paste(best_cv, "minus", n), mean_diff_ROC = mean(d),
             low = unname(quantile(d, 0.025)), high = unname(quantile(d, 0.975)))
}))
diffs[, -1] <- round(diffs[, -1], 3)
knitr::kable(diffs, caption = "Paired ROC-AUC differences against the model chosen by cross-validation")
```

## ROC and precision-recall curves

```{r curves, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
curve_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(probs), function(n) {
  k <- pr_curve(probs[[n]], yte); data.frame(model = n, k)
}))
roc_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(curve_df, curve_df$model), function(d)
  rbind(data.frame(model = d$model[1], fpr = 0, recall = 0), d[, c("model", "fpr", "recall")])))
ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, recall, colour = model)) + geom_line() +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(title = "ROC curves (test)", x = "False positive rate", y = "Sensitivity") + theme_minimal()
ggplot(curve_df, aes(recall, precision, colour = model)) + geom_step() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = prev, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(title = "Precision-recall curves (test); dashed line = prevalence",
       x = "Recall (sensitivity)", y = "Precision (PPV)") + ylim(0, 1) + theme_minimal()
```

## What happens to ROC-AUC and PR-AUC if the disease is rarer?

I re-weight the test patients who lived so that deaths make up 5% of the
population. Sensitivity and specificity do not change; precision does.

```{r rare}
w5 <- (sum(yte == "Died") * 0.95 / 0.05) / sum(yte == "Living")   # weight per survivor
rare_tab <- t(sapply(probs, function(p) c(
  ROC_AUC_at_test_prev = roc_auc(p, yte), ROC_AUC_at_5pct = roc_auc(p, yte),
  PR_AUC_at_test_prev = pr_auc(p, yte), PR_AUC_at_5pct = pr_auc(p, yte, w_neg = w5))))
knitr::kable(round(rare_tab, 3))
```

## A threshold chosen for sensitivity (on training data only)

A threshold of 0.5 is arbitrary. For each model I take the **out-of-fold**
training predictions and choose the highest threshold that still catches at
least 85% of the deaths, then apply it unchanged to the test set.

```{r threshold}
pick_thr <- function(m, target = 0.85) {
  d <- m$pred
  d <- aggregate(Died ~ rowIndex + obs, data = d, FUN = mean)   # average over repeats
  th <- sort(unique(d$Died), decreasing = TRUE)
  sens <- sapply(th, function(t) mean(d$Died[d$obs == "Died"] >= t))
  th[which(sens >= target)[1]]
}
thr <- sapply(models, pick_thr)
thr_tab <- t(sapply(names(models), function(n) {
  mm <- confusion(probs[[n]], yte, thr[[n]]); a <- all_metrics(probs[[n]], yte, thr[[n]])
  c(threshold = thr[[n]], sensitivity = a[["sensitivity"]], specificity = a[["specificity"]],
    PPV = safe(mm[["TP"]], mm[["TP"]] + mm[["FP"]]), missed_deaths = mm[["FN"]], false_alarms = mm[["FP"]])
}))
knitr::kable(round(thr_tab, 3), caption = "Test results at the sensitivity-targeted thresholds")
```

```{r interpret, fig.height=4}
or_tab <- data.frame(term = rownames(co), odds_ratio_per_SD = exp(co[, 1]),

```

```{r separation}
table(SHANK2_mutated = feat_tr$SHANK2, outcome = ytr)
```

The `SHANK2` odds ratio has an impossibly wide interval because of
**quasi-separation**: look at the table above. That coefficient should not be read
or quoted. `BREAST_SURGERY` (mastectomy) probably stands for tumour extent (bigger
or more advanced tumours more often need mastectomy), so it is not a reason to
operate differently.

# 3. Recommendation

```{r rec-numbers, include=FALSE}
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
cvv <- setNames(cv_tab$cv_ROC_AUC, cv_tab$model)
lr <- "Logistic regression"
lt <- thr_tab[lr, ]
```

**Use logistic regression, only to prompt discussion, never to decide
treatment.** Cross-validation cannot separate the top models (ROC-AUC
`r f2(cvv["Random forest"])` random forest, `r f2(cvv["SVM (radial)"])` SVM,
`r f2(cvv[lr])` logistic; gaps under one standard deviation), so I prefer the one
a clinician can inspect. Its test ROC-AUC (`r f2(metric_mat[lr, "ROC_AUC"])`) and
PR-AUC (`r f2(metric_mat[lr, "PR_AUC"])`) were also highest, though intervals
overlap.

**Metric:** sensitivity, always beside specificity. At a training-chosen
threshold it caught `r sum(yte == "Died") - lt[["missed_deaths"]]` of
`r sum(yte == "Died")` deaths but flagged `r lt[["false_alarms"]]` of
`r sum(yte == "Living")` survivors (specificity `r f2(lt[["specificity"]])`, PPV
`r f2(lt[["PPV"]])` against prevalence `r f2(prev)`). That is little better than
calling everyone high risk, so it must not justify withholding or reducing
therapy.

**What would change my mind:** a larger external cohort where another model beats
it in paired ROC-AUC or PR-AUC with an interval excluding zero; specificity of at
least 0.50 at 85% sensitivity; and good calibration. Until then, none of these
models is ready for clinical use.

# Written answers

## 1. Why accuracy misleads here

```{r q1, include=FALSE}
acc_base <- metric_mat["Majority-class baseline", "accuracy"]
best_acc_name <- rownames(metric_mat)[-1][which.max(metric_mat[-1, "accuracy"])]
best_acc <- metric_mat[best_acc_name, "accuracy"]
extra <- round((best_acc - acc_base) * n_test)
```

The baseline that predicts "Living" for everyone scores
**`r round(100 * acc_base, 1)`% accuracy** on the test set
(`r sum(yte == "Living")` of `r n_test`) while catching **0 of
`r sum(yte == "Died")` deaths** (sensitivity 0, balanced accuracy 0.50, F1 0). The
highest accuracy of my four models is the `r best_acc_name`'s
`r round(100 * best_acc, 1)`%, which sounds respectable but is only
`r round(100 * (best_acc - acc_base), 1)` points, about **`r extra` more patients**,
above doing nothing. It still misses `r conf_mat[best_acc_name, "FN"]` of the
`r sum(yte == "Died")` deaths (sensitivity `r f2(metric_mat[best_acc_name, "sensitivity"])`).
Logistic regression is worse on accuracy
(`r round(100 * metric_mat[lr, "accuracy"], 1)`%, only
`r round((metric_mat[lr, "accuracy"] - acc_base) * n_test)` patients above the
baseline). The tree and the forest have identical confusion matrices at 0.5 and so
identical accuracy, yet different ROC-AUC
(`r f2(metric_mat["Decision tree", "ROC_AUC"])` against
`r f2(metric_mat["Random forest", "ROC_AUC"])`): accuracy cannot even see that.
Accuracy mixes the two kinds of error, weighs them equally, depends on the class
mix and on one arbitrary threshold. Balanced accuracy, sensitivity and
specificity show what is hidden.

## 2. ROC-AUC against PR-AUC

ROC-AUC compares sensitivity with the false-positive rate. Both are calculated
*within* a true class, so ROC-AUC **does not change with prevalence**, and its
chance level is always 0.50. PR-AUC uses precision, which depends on how many
negatives there are, so its chance level **is the prevalence**. They disagree
mainly when the positive class is rare: many false positives barely move the
false-positive rate but wreck precision.

On my test set the death rate is `r round(100 * prev, 1)`%, close to balanced, and
the two **agree on the ranking**: logistic regression
(ROC `r f2(metric_mat[lr, "ROC_AUC"])`, PR `r f2(metric_mat[lr, "PR_AUC"])`), then
SVM (`r f2(metric_mat["SVM (radial)", "ROC_AUC"])`,
`r f2(metric_mat["SVM (radial)", "PR_AUC"])`), random forest
(`r f2(metric_mat["Random forest", "ROC_AUC"])`,
`r f2(metric_mat["Random forest", "PR_AUC"])`) and tree
(`r f2(metric_mat["Decision tree", "ROC_AUC"])`,
`r f2(metric_mat["Decision tree", "PR_AUC"])`). Remember the baselines: 0.50 for
ROC and `r f2(prev)` for PR. When I re-weight to 5% prevalence, ROC-AUC is
unchanged but PR-AUC falls to `r f2(rare_tab[lr, "PR_AUC_at_5pct"])` for logistic
regression and `r f2(min(rare_tab[, "PR_AUC_at_5pct"]))`-`r f2(sort(rare_tab[, "PR_AUC_at_5pct"], decreasing = TRUE)[2])` for the others, and the tree and
forest swap places.

**Which to trust:** the question is about the patients who die, so I give more
weight to **PR-AUC read against its prevalence baseline**, and especially if the
model were used where deaths are rarer than in this cohort. At this cohort's
prevalence they tell the same story. Neither is precise: with
`r sum(yte == "Died")` deaths the 95% interval for logistic PR-AUC is
`r ci$PR_low[ci$model == lr]`-`r ci$PR_high[ci$model == lr]`. The 5% figures rest on
very few top-ranked patients, so treat them as an illustration.

## 3. What the two errors mean for a patient

* **False negative:** a patient who will die of the disease is called low risk.
  The board might lean towards less intensive therapy or less follow-up, and the
  patient may lose the chance of treatment escalation or a clinical trial. The
  harm can be irreversible.
* **False positive:** a patient who would survive is called high risk. They may
  receive more intensive treatment than they need, with real harms (infection from
  low blood counts, nerve damage, heart toxicity from some drugs), plus anxiety
  and cost. Some harm is lasting, but it does not by itself leave a cancer
  under-treated.

**I would report sensitivity first**, at a threshold fixed before looking at the
test data, and **never without specificity** next to it, because sensitivity of
100% is free if you call everyone high risk. For a patient the next number is the
predictive value *at the local prevalence* (question 4). AUCs are for comparing
models; they do not tell a clinician what happens to the person in front of them.

## 4. Positive predictive value at two prevalences

By Bayes' rule, PPV = (sens x prev) / (sens x prev + (1 - spec) x (1 - prev)).

```{r ppv}
ppv <- function(se, sp, pr) se * pr / (se * pr + (1 - sp) * (1 - pr))
npv <- function(se, sp, pr) sp * (1 - pr) / (sp * (1 - pr) + (1 - se) * pr)
pts <- list("threshold 0.5" = all_metrics(probs[[lr]], yte, 0.5),
            "sensitivity-targeted threshold" = all_metrics(probs[[lr]], yte, thr[[lr]]))
ppv_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pts), function(n) {
  se <- pts[[n]][["sensitivity"]]; sp <- pts[[n]][["specificity"]]
  data.frame(operating_point = n, sensitivity = se, specificity = sp,
             PPV_at_data_prevalence = ppv(se, sp, mean(dat$y == "Died")),
             PPV_at_5pct = ppv(se, sp, 0.05),
             NPV_at_data_prevalence = npv(se, sp, mean(dat$y == "Died")),
             NPV_at_5pct = npv(se, sp, 0.05))
}))
ppv_tab[, -1] <- round(ppv_tab[, -1], 3)
knitr::kable(ppv_tab, caption = "Logistic regression: predictive values (data prevalence = all 190 patients)")
```

The prevalence in my data is `r round(100 * mean(dat$y == "Died"), 1)`% (83 of
190). At the sensitivity-targeted threshold the PPV is
**`r ppv_tab$PPV_at_data_prevalence[2]`** there but only
**`r ppv_tab$PPV_at_5pct[2]`** at 5% prevalence: about
**`r round(1 / ppv_tab$PPV_at_5pct[2])` patients flagged for each one who would
actually die**. At threshold 0.5 the PPV goes from
`r ppv_tab$PPV_at_data_prevalence[1]` to `r ppv_tab$PPV_at_5pct[1]`.

**Effect on the recommendation:** in a low-risk population the model's "high risk"
label would be wrong for the large majority, so it must not be moved to a
different setting without recalibrating and re-choosing the threshold. The high
NPV at 5% (`r ppv_tab$NPV_at_5pct[2]`) is not an achievement: 95% of such people
survive anyway. This makes my recommendation narrower: discussion support in a
population like this one, and no use at all for screening or low-risk groups.
(Death-from-disease prevalence also depends on the length of follow-up, so a
number from this cohort does not transfer directly.)

## 5. If the best performer is hardest to explain

Here the cross-validation leader is the **random forest**
(`r f2(cvv["Random forest"])`), with the SVM close behind; both are hard to
explain. Logistic regression is `r round(cvv["Random forest"] - cvv[lr], 3)` lower
in cross-validation, less than the fold-to-fold standard deviation
(`r f2(cv_tab$cv_ROC_sd[cv_tab$model == lr])`), and on the test set the paired
difference (forest minus logistic) is
`r diffs$mean_diff_ROC[diffs$comparison == "Random forest minus Logistic regression"]`
with a 95% interval of
`r diffs$low[diffs$comparison == "Random forest minus Logistic regression"]` to
`r diffs$high[diffs$comparison == "Random forest minus Logistic regression"]`,
which includes zero. The forest may also have had a small head start, because it
helped choose the features.

**To a clinician I would recommend logistic regression** and say this: "Higher
nodal-prognostic score (NPI), mastectomy and a `MAP3K1` mutation went with higher
odds of death in these patients (odds ratios per standard deviation
`r or_tab$odds_ratio_per_SD[or_tab$term == "NPI"]`,
`r or_tab$odds_ratio_per_SD[or_tab$term == "BREAST_SURGERY.MASTECTOMY"]` and
`r or_tab$odds_ratio_per_SD[or_tab$term == "MAP3K1"]`; the NPI interval includes 1).
These are associations, not causes, and the mutation findings are based on very
few patients."

**What I give up:** possibly a small amount of discrimination (up to about
`r round(cvv["Random forest"] - cvv[lr], 2)` in cross-validated ROC-AUC, which I
cannot show to be real), and any non-linear effects or interactions the forest or
SVM might capture. **What I gain:** each input's effect can be read and
challenged, the score can be written down and audited, and an odd coefficient
shows up, as the `SHANK2` one did, instead of hiding inside a black box. If a
larger external study showed the forest clearly and consistently better, I would
change the recommendation and add explanation tools, while telling the clinician
those explanations are approximations of the model, not its reasoning.
